1 · Start here

Build the causal chain first

Dr. Harris repeatedly frames this lecture as a “tie-it-together” lecture. The recurring exam skill is to identify which hemodynamic variable changed and then predict what backs up, what compensates, and what eventually fails.

Repeatable question approach

  1. Name the primary failure: contraction, relaxation/compliance, RV afterload, or a precipitant.
  2. Identify the altered variable: preload, afterload, contractility, heart rate, or compliance.
  3. Predict SV/CO and filling pressure. Ask: does more blood remain behind? Is the ventricle harder to fill?
  4. Trace the backup: LV → LA → pulmonary veins/capillaries → dyspnea; or RV/RA → systemic veins → JVD/edema/liver/ascites.
  5. Add compensation: Frank-Starling, hypertrophy/remodeling, SNS, RAAS, ADH.
  6. Ask when compensation turns harmful: ↑ preload, ↑ afterload, tachycardia/MVO₂, fibrosis/remodeling.
  7. Match the figure: ESPVR change = contractility; EDPVR change = compliance; right-edge/EDV change = preload; taller/narrower loop with ↑ESV = afterload.

Professor emphasis → exam priority

  • Frank-Starling relationship: especially why extra preload eventually produces congestion rather than useful output.
  • PV loops: timing + preload/afterload/contractility + HFrEF vs HFpEF.
  • “Good → bad” compensation: SNS, RAAS/Ang II, ADH, hypertrophy/remodeling.
  • Left vs right congestion: pulmonary vs systemic venous findings.
  • Precipitants + staging: recognize what pushes a compensated patient over the edge.

2 · Mechanisms

Predict the next consequence

All graphics in the interactive explorers are schematic teaching models, not patient recordings or measured values.

Normal physiology → HF logic

VariableLecture meaningDirection that usually helps SV
PreloadEnd-diastolic stretch / ventricular filling↑ helps within Frank-Starling reserve; too much → congestion
AfterloadForce/pressure that must be overcome to eject↓ generally helps a weak LV eject
ContractilityForce independent of initial fiber length and afterload↑ → steeper ESPVR, ↓ESV, ↑SV
ComplianceEase of filling at a given pressure↑ compliance → lower filling pressure for a given volume
Professor self-correction: lowering afterload can improve ejection/stroke volume, but it does not necessarily increase intrinsic contractility. The Q&A explicitly clarified this.

Why compensation becomes decompensation

  1. ↓ CO is sensed as inadequate perfusion.
  2. SNS → ↑HR/contractility + arterial/venous constriction.
  3. RAAS/ADH → vasoconstriction + Na⁺/water retention + thirst.
  4. Short term: pressure and perfusion are defended.
  5. Long term: ↑afterload + ↑preload + tachycardia/MVO₂ + remodeling/fibrosis.
  6. Result: even lower effective output and higher filling pressures → more activation.

5 · Recognition lab

Turn findings back into physiology

Back-up map

PV-loop recognition rules

  • Right edge moves right with same ESPVR → think ↑ preload.
  • ESV moves right + loop narrows/tallens with same ESPVR → think ↑ afterload.
  • ESPVR steeper + ESV moves left → think ↑ contractility.
  • ESPVR flatter + ESV/EDV increase → HFrEF / systolic dysfunction.
  • EDPVR up/left → reduced compliance / HFpEF physiology.

Stage A vs B vs C vs D

A: risk, no structural disease/symptoms.

B: structural/functional abnormality, no symptoms.

C: current or prior HF symptoms + structural disease.

D: advanced/refractory symptoms despite therapy.

NYHA I → IV

I: no activity limitation.

II: symptoms with moderate exertion.

III: symptoms with minimal exertion.

IV: symptoms at rest.

Precipitant classifier

Demand: infection/fever, anemia, tachycardia, hyperthyroid, pregnancy.

Preload: sodium/fluid excess, renal failure.

Afterload: uncontrolled HTN; PE → RV afterload.

Contractility: ischemia/MI, negative inotrope, excess alcohol.

Heart-sound clarification

Lecture Dr. Harris correctly emphasizes that S3 and S4 are both diastolic in timing. The transcript then describes S3 as a “concussion splash on a stiff myocardium,” which is imprecise.

Supplemental clarification Standard physiology: S3 = early rapid filling / volume-overload pattern; S4 = atrial contraction into a stiff, noncompliant ventricle. Use this mechanistic distinction for exams.

8 · Exam sheet

One-pass final review

Core equations

CO = HR × SV
SV = EDV − ESV
EF = (EDV − ESV) / EDV
BP = CO × TPR
Wall stress σ = P×r/(2h)

Three SV determinants

Preload ↑ → SV ↑ within physiologic reserve.
Afterload ↑ → ESV ↑, SV ↓.
Contractility ↑ → ESPVR steeper, ESV ↓, SV ↑.

HFrEF vs HFpEF

HFrEF: impaired contraction, flatter ESPVR, ↑ESV/EDV, ↓SV/EF.
HFpEF: impaired relaxation/compliance, EDPVR up/left, higher filling pressure, preserved EF.

Both cause dyspnea: elevated LV filling pressure → LA → pulmonary veins/capillaries → edema.

Left vs right

Left: dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, rales, pulmonary congestion.
Right: JVD, dependent edema, hepatomegaly/RUQ discomfort, ascites.

#1 cause right HF: left HF. Cor pulmonale: right HF from primary pulmonary disease.

Compensation → harm

SNS: ↑HR/contractility initially; chronic tachycardia + vasoconstriction → ↑MVO₂ + ↑afterload.
RAAS: vasoconstriction + aldosterone/thirst → ↑afterload + ↑preload; Ang II also drives remodeling.
ADH: water retention → ↑volume/preload.
Hypertrophy: helps wall stress initially → stiffness/fibrosis later.

Natriuretic peptides

BNP rises with ventricular hemodynamic stress. ANP/BNP → Na⁺/water excretion, vasodilation, renin inhibition, antagonism of Ang II effects on aldosterone/vasopressin.

PV-loop recognition

ESPVR slope changed? contractility.
EDPVR shifted up/left? stiffness/HFpEF.
EDV/right edge increased? preload.
ESV ↑ with same ESPVR? afterload.

Lecture PCWP threshold

Slide 19: 3–12 normal, 12–25 elevated, >25 mm Hg pulmonary edema. Treat this as the professor’s slide-specific threshold.

Stages + NYHA

A: risk. B: structural disease, no symptoms. C: current/prior symptoms. D: refractory/advanced.
NYHA I: none. II: moderate exertion. III: minimal exertion. IV: rest.

Precipitants

Demand ↑: infection/fever, anemia, tachycardia, hyperthyroid, pregnancy.
Preload ↑: sodium/fluid excess, renal failure.
Afterload ↑: HTN; PE → RV afterload.
Contractility ↓: ischemia/MI, negative inotrope, alcohol.
Also: medication nonadherence, excessive bradycardia.

Common traps

  • Afterload reduction improves ejection; it does not directly increase intrinsic contractility.
  • Preserved EF does not mean normal filling pressure.
  • S3 and S4 are both diastolic; S3 = rapid filling/volume pattern, S4 = atrial kick into stiff ventricle.
  • More preload is not always better on a failing Frank-Starling curve.
  • Do not call all right HF “cor pulmonale.”
9 · Sources & clarifications

What came from lecture vs supplemental verification

Provided materials used

  • Harris-Pathophysiology_of_Congestive_Heart_Failure_2026.pptx — all 40 slides reviewed; 15 slide images embedded here.
  • Pathophysiology of C-transcript.txt — used for professor emphasis, causal explanations, Q&A clarifications, and material described conversationally.
  • Harris_Pathophysiology_of_Congestive_Heart_Failure_2026.docx — learning objectives and assigned readings.
  • Pathophysiology_of_Congestive_Heart_Failure_-_Practice_Questions.docx — three professor practice questions and answer key.
  • Professor Poll Everywhere questions on slides 38–40 were included as professor-source practice.

Adaptations

Professor questions are labeled as professor-source. “Adapted” questions preserve lecture reasoning but change the entry point. “Original” questions were written only from lecture concepts unless explicitly marked with a clarification. The interactive PV/Frank-Starling graphics are schematic reconstructions, not original lecture figures or measured clinical data.

Meaningful clarifications

1) HF definition. Slide 13 describes CHF as failure to pump adequate blood flow to maintain tissue perfusion. That is useful for the lecture’s low-output framework but is narrower than current definitions, which include impairment of ventricular filling or ejection and can include preserved EF. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline; 2026 Second Universal Definition.

2) S3 vs S4 mechanism. The professor correctly states both occur in diastole, but the transcript’s description of S3 as a splash on a “stiff myocardium” is imprecise. Standard references describe S3 during early rapid filling/volume-overload patterns and S4 during atrial contraction into a noncompliant ventricle. NCBI: Heart Sounds; NCBI: Fourth Heart Sound.

3) Afterload vs contractility. Early in the transcript, afterload reduction is described as making the heart “squeeze better.” In the student Q&A, Dr. Harris explicitly clarifies that lower afterload allows greater ejection against a lower load but does not necessarily change intrinsic contractility. This Lab uses the Q&A clarification.

4) Stage terminology. The lecture’s A–D staging remains conceptually aligned with modern staging; current terminology names A “At Risk,” B “Pre-HF,” C “Symptomatic HF,” and D “Advanced HF.”

5) PCWP threshold. Slide 19’s 3–12 / 12–25 / >25 mm Hg ranges are preserved for lecture-specific testing. Clinical interpretation depends on context; do not treat a single threshold as a universal standalone diagnostic rule.

Scope note: This is a pathophysiology lecture, not a comprehensive heart-failure pharmacotherapy lecture. The treatment sections therefore emphasize the lecture’s physiologic rationale (afterload, volume, RAAS/neurohormonal signaling, precipitants) without silently importing a full modern GDMT regimen.
